text.p: Following are the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Wednesday.
VJESNIK
- Croatia and Italy signed accords on the protection of ethnic minorities in both countries, and on the promotion and protection of bilateral investments.

- Croatia has now formally become a member of the Council of Europe. This opens the door for various processes such as negotiations with WTO and CEFTA, and admission to Partnership for Peace most probably as soon as in January 1997.
- State oil company INA is to begin exporting its diesel fuel soon.
- VAT may not be imposed before the presidential elections in summer 1997, as public dissatisfaction with it seems to grow.
- Electric board HEP is to build an Adriatic thermoelectric plant in Lukovo Sugarje, south of Karlobag.
- Employers' association (HUP) proposes to set up an agency which should help crediting small and medium-sized enterprises.
VECERNJI LIST
- Economic cooperation between Croatia and Bosnia is increasing. Croatia's exports totalled $225 million last year, and imports jumped from meagre six million in 1995 to 30 million so far this year.
- Commercial banks to take over payments from central bureau next year, but many technicalities remain unresolved.
- Higher prices of seasonal products caused retail prices to go up 0.6 percent in October but anaylists believe there is no danger of rising inflation.
- Stock market: Only blue chips resisted the downward trend during the past week.
- Money market: Liquidity is good, but October lending rates were significantly higher than the month before.
- VAT debate: some speculate that Finance Ministry might scrap the rate for basic consumables.
SLOBODNA DALMACIJA
- I believe Blaskic is innocent, says Anto Nobilo, Zagreb lawyer who takes over the defence of Bosnian Croat general Tihofil Blaskic at the Hague war crimes tribunal.
- London still has to give back some of the Yugoslav gold, confiscated by the allies after World War Two, and which was returned in part to the then authorities between 1958 and 1982.

- Commentary: What is the true Croatian reality? One can hardly speak about an economic miracle in a country where one fourth of the population lives in poverty, almost every fifth citizens is jobless and 14 percent receive some form of social aid.
- President Tudjman receives representatives of the Serb Orthodox Church in a step towards reconciliation. -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
